prompt: I run Tidewater Kayak Rentals and need the booking summary card for our checkout page. It shows the trip name (Saturday sunrise paddle), date and meeting time, three line items (single kayak $45, dry bag $8, photo package $15), the total, a Confirm booking button and a small Change dates link. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts and no external assets.
rubric: The card's outer padding in the CSS is between 16 and 32 px, and no side of the content touches the card edge.
The Confirm booking button is between 36 and 48 px tall (height or padding plus line height) and the Change dates link is visibly lower in emphasis than the button.

Spacing between the trip name and its date/time is clearly smaller than the space between the details block, the line items and the total area, so the card reads as groups rather than evenly spaced lines.
Spacing values in the CSS come from a small repeating set of round numbers (steps of 4, plus an occasional 6 or 10); there are no scattered one-off values such as 13, 19 or 27 px.
Prices are right-aligned in one column and the total is separated from the line items by a rule or a larger gap, not just another equal row.

prompt: Make the notification settings page for Fernlight, an app that monitors home greenhouses. Three areas: Alerts (frost warning, low soil moisture, door left open, each with a short explanation and an on/off switch), Schedule (a quiet-hours start and end time and a daily summary time) and Account (email address field and a Save changes button). Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts and no external assets.
rubric: The three areas are visibly separated from each other by a larger gap, rule or tinted region than the gap between rows inside an area.
Within each alert row the label and its explanation sit closer together than the row sits to the next row.
All on/off switches share one right-hand (or left-hand) edge, and the time and email inputs share a common width or aligned edge.
Inputs and the Save changes button are between 32 and 48 px tall, with the same height for inputs that sit on the same line.
The page has no horizontal overflow at a 1280 px wide viewport and the content column is capped to a readable width rather than stretching edge to edge.
The card's padding is raised into roughly the 12 to 24 px range and line-height for the text is at least 1.3.
The button is between 32 and 44 px tall and has at least 8 px of space between it and the Report a problem link (or the link is moved to its own line).
The customer name, items and shelf location read as one related group with gaps between them of roughly 2 to 8 px, set apart from the heading and from the actions by a bigger gap.
The replacement values come from round steps (multiples of 2 or 4, with 6 or 10 allowed); the fix does not introduce odd values like 5, 7, 9, 11 or 13 px.
The markup and wording are left unchanged, and the answer is the updated CSS rather than a redesign.

prompt: I'm building the top bar for Switchback, a trail-running log. Logo on the left, three text links (Runs, Routes, Gear), and a Log a run button on the right. My last attempt looked tiny and cramped next to the big hero photo underneath. Give me the CSS for the bar and the button with real numbers, not 'it depends'.
rubric: The CSS gives the bar a concrete height or padding that resolves to roughly 56 to 88 px tall.
The Log a run button is given a concrete height between 32 and 44 px and horizontal padding that is at least about half its height.
Link spacing is a concrete gap or padding (for example 16 to 32 px between links), and the logo, links and button are vertically centered on one line.
All numbers are clean round values (steps of 4, with 6 or 10 allowed for small nudges); the answer does not invent values such as 53 px or 17 px, or insist that every number be a multiple of 8.
The answer is short and mostly CSS with a sentence or two of reasoning, not a long design lecture.
The review points out that the label sits 24 px away from its own input while fields are only 12 px apart, so each label reads as belonging to the field above it.
The review does not flag the 4, 6, 10, 12 and 24 px values themselves, or ask for them to be moved onto an 8 px grid or a different scale.
The review says plainly that the rest of the spacing (padding, button and input heights, section gaps) is fine and should be left alone.
Any fix is concrete (a specific new label gap in roughly the 4 to 8 px range) and limited to the label spacing, with no wholesale rewrite.
The answer is a short list of findings rather than a long audit of every rule.
The answer says the spacing already works and that little or nothing needs to change, rather than finding something to fix on principle.
At most two small edits are proposed, each with a stated reason that can be checked in the CSS; no wholesale rewrite or restyling.
Padding stays in roughly the 16 to 24 px range, the button stays between 40 and 48 px tall, and the route/time pair stays tighter than the gap to the meta row.
The answer does not invent problems (for example it does not claim the 4, 12, 16 or 20 px values are inconsistent) and does not change the markup.

prompt: The night-shift pharmacy at Ashgrove Clinic keeps a dispensing log open on a 1366 by 768 laptop next to other windows. Build the log page with 24 made-up entries (time, patient initials, drug and strength, quantity, technician). They want to see as many entries as possible at once without squinting. Give me one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts and no external assets.
rubric: At a 1366 by 768 viewport at least 16 entries are visible without scrolling, which in the CSS means row heights of roughly 28 to 36 px.
Vertical cell padding is compact (roughly 4 to 10 px) while body text stays at 13 px or larger.
Columns are left-aligned for text and right-aligned for quantity, the header row is visually distinct, and the table uses the page width without horizontal scrolling.
Rows are distinguished by a thin rule or light zebra tint rather than by extra whitespace, and spacing is the same on every row.
The page does not wrap the table in a large padded card or add a hero or summary block that pushes entries below the fold.
The answer is three sentences or fewer and under about 90 words in total.
It identifies that almost no space separates the content from the footer (footer margin is 0 and the last section's margin is only 8 px) and that the footer's own padding is tight.
It proposes one concrete change with a value in roughly the 24 to 64 px range, for example a margin-top or padding on the footer.
It does not add a list of extra recommendations, a rewritten stylesheet or a lecture on spacing theory.
The answer picks one version clearly (B) instead of saying both are fine.
The reasoning is tied to visible gaps in the CSS: in A every gap is 16 px so title, level, blurb and button all run together, while B keeps the title and level tight and sets the button apart.
It does not recommend either version because of a grid or a multiple-of-8 rule, and does not mark B's 4, 12 or 20 px values as mistakes.
If it suggests a tweak, the tweak is small and specific (one value changed) rather than a redesign of B.
The answer is brief: a clear pick, a few sentences of reasons.

prompt:
My signup form looks like one big blob even though I gave everything the same margin to keep it consistent. Why does it look like that and what would you change?

Join the Larkspur Cycling Club

form > * { margin-bottom: 16px; display: block; }
rubric: It explains that equal spacing everywhere means labels, inputs, field pairs and the button are all the same distance apart, so nothing groups with anything.
It recommends a small gap between each label and its input (about 4 to 8 px) and a larger gap between fields (about 16 to 24 px).
It suggests grouping the related fields (about you, ride details, emergency contact) with a bigger gap or a divider of roughly 24 to 48 px between groups, and giving the button extra space above it.
It gives its fix as concrete CSS or numbers and does not tell the user that consistent margins were a mistake in themselves.
Values suggested are round numbers, and the answer stays focused on this form.
